title: Into your hands (Luke 23:44–56)
hookLine: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit; the women prepare spices
carry: even in grief, keep the sabbath
tomorrow: why seek the living among the dead?
last: THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.

cards: Some prayers are learned so early they're there when nothing else is. At the end, the line Jesus reaches for comes from Psalm thirty-one.

It's about the sixth hour, around noon, and Luke says darkness covers the whole land until the ninth hour, around three. The sun's light fails. In the temple, the curtain of the sanctuary is torn down the middle.
And Jesus, who has been praying all through this Gospel, prays one last time, with a line from the prayers of his people.

teach.b: In the King James words: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost." Commend means to hand over, to entrust, the way you'd give someone you love into another's care.
The psalm reads: "Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth." Jesus adds one word to the front of it: Father.
In Mark and Matthew, his last words from the cross come from a different psalm, my God, why hast thou forsaken me. Luke gives this one instead.
Christians keep both, and some hear two sides of the same death: the cry of abandonment, and the word of trust. Then Luke turns to the people watching.

A Roman centurion glorifies God and says, "Certainly this was a righteous man." The crowds go home beating their breasts. His friends, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stand at a distance and watch.
Then Joseph, from Arimathea, steps forward: a member of the council who, Luke tells us, hadn't agreed with their decision.

teach.h: INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.
teach.b: He asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a tomb cut into rock, where no one had ever been laid. The women follow and see where. They go home and prepare spices and ointments.
And then, Luke says, they rested on the sabbath, according to the commandment. Even in grief, they keep the sabbath, and wait.

how: In Compline, the church's night prayer, the words 'into thy hands' are said or sung as the day ends, and on Good Friday the last words from the cross are read and remembered.

the garden where Jesus was arrested at night
the hometown of Joseph, who buried Jesus

games.q: what's inside Luke 23:44–56 — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus's last words are the same in every Gospel
in Mark and Matthew he cries 'why hast thou forsaken me'; in Luke, 'into thy hands I commend my spirit'.
Joseph of Arimathea was a member of the council
Luke says he had not consented to their counsel and deed.
the women rested on the sabbath before going to the tomb
they rested the sabbath day according to the commandment.

games.q: you're Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who disagreed with its decision. Jesus is dead, and the sabbath is near. what do you do?
o: ask Pilate for the body and lay it in a new tomb.
denounce the council in the street.
games.why: he goes to Pilate, begs the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a rock tomb where no one had ever been laid.

practice: Think of what you'll carry into bed tonight: your tired body, your worries, the people you love. Imagine opening your hands and placing each one into hands larger than yours, without needing to know how it will turn out.
If you pray, you can say it now and again before sleep, into thy hands I commend my spirit; if you don't, simply open your hands on your lap and let the day go.

wordCard.voice: Arimathea. The town of Joseph, the council member who didn't agree with Jesus's death sentence and asked Pilate for his body to bury it in a new tomb.

orig.note: Greek: I entrust, I hand over into someone's keeping. Luke's word for 'I commend'.

carryVoice: Your line: even in grief, keep the sabbath. The spices were ready, and the rest came first. Day five hundred eighty-seven, done.
